analysis.one_liner: Requires independent commissions to draw congressional districts and open primaries for federal elections.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; despite having a Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, it sat in two House committees until the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have taken the drawing of congressional district lines away from state politicians and given it to independent commissions whose members cannot hold elected office and must be politically balanced, starting with the 2020 census. It also would have required open primaries for federal elections, so any registered voter could vote in any party's primary. States would have been barred from using federal election-administration money unless they adopted the same rules for their own legislative districts and local primaries.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters gain two ways. First, districts drawn by politicians tend to be safe for one party or the other, so general elections are uncompetitive and the real choice happens in a low-turnout primary; independent commissions aim to produce districts where the general election actually decides who serves. Second, open primaries would let independent voters — who are barred from voting in many states' closed primaries — help choose the candidates. Challengers of both parties and minor-party or independent candidates would face fairer terrain. The people who lose are the incumbents who currently draw their own lines and the party organizations that control who votes in primaries.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, especially independents and those in gerrymandered districts

how_it_helps.text: Takes congressional redistricting away from state politicians: beginning with the 2020 census, each state must use a plan developed by an independent redistricting commission whose members cannot be elected officials and whose partisan makeup must be balanced
Requires open primaries for federal elections, meaning any registered voter could cast a ballot in any party's primary, including for presidential delegates and conventions

Conditions federal election-administration money on states applying the same reforms to their own state legislative districts and state and local primaries, certified to the Election Assistance Commission — pushing the anti-gerrymandering rules down to the state level

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislators of both parties, who currently draw their own district lines and benefit from safe seats. State political parties lose their ability to restrict primary participation to registered party members. States that refuse to comply would forfeit federal election-administration funds, and all states would bear the cost of building commissions and switching primary systems.

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state control over elections: the Constitution gives states the primary role in running their own elections, and conditioning federal election-administration money on states rewriting their redistricting and primary laws is a blunt federal mandate that some states would refuse on principle, forfeiting that funding

Open primaries allow voters of any party — or no party — to vote in any party's primary, which critics say enables crossover interference (members of one party influencing the other party's nominee) and weakens party organizations' ability to choose their own candidates

The definition of an acceptable commission is thin — it only requires partisan balance and no elected officeholders, and says nothing about how members are selected or how fair the maps must be — so a state could stack a formally 'balanced' commission that still produces favorable lines

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: voters in gerrymandered states would get competitive elections and independents would get a primary ballot, while incumbent officeholders and party organizations give up structural advantages that keep them in power. The costs are mostly institutional, not financial for ordinary people, though the funding condition is coercive and could leave election administration underfunded in noncompliant states, and the commission standards could have been tighter. On balance this is a straightforward pro-voter reform whose main price is paid by the officeholders it would have regulated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or a vote in either one, and expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a Pennsylvania Republican, introduced the CLEAN Elections Act on January 3, 2019, the first day of the 116th Congress
It was referred to the House Administration Committee and the Judiciary Committee, and then to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties
Only one House Democrat signed on as a cosponsor — two members of the House in total — and neither committee ever acted on the bill

No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the 2020 redistricting cycle proceeded under each state's existing, politician-controlled processes

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislators of both parties came out ahead: the bill expired before it could have taken away their power to draw district lines or restrict primary participation, and the 2020 redistricting that followed remained in politicians' hands.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape never showed itself; the only recorded support was a lone Republican sponsor plus one Democratic cosponsor, and it is not known how the rest of either party would have voted.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislators
industries.note: Politicians in most states currently draw the district lines they will run in, which reliably produces safe seats; the bill would strip that power and hand it to balanced, non-officeholder commissions. Their interest in keeping the pen runs directly against voters' interest in competitive elections.

Closed primaries give party organizations control over who participates in choosing nominees — usually the only election that matters in safe districts. Open primaries would let any registered voter, including independents, vote in any party's primary.

States would have to build independent commissions and switch to open primaries, or lose federal election-administration money — a real administrative and fiscal burden. Compliant states would keep their federal election funding.
